explication:
<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose  
   - Apollo is a native C++17-based streaming server (desktop stream host) with an integrated web UI.  
   - Purpose: host low-latency game streams for Artemis/Moonlight clients, manage virtual displays, input, encoding (HW/SW), and client permissions.

2. Analyze the file structure  
   - src/ : core server modules (network, HTTP, RTSP, UPnP, config, crypto, audio/video, input, logging, task/thread pools, virtual display management).  
   - src/platform/ : OS-specific abstractions (Windows via SudoVDA & DirectX, Linux via VAAPI/Wayland/X11, macOS via AVFoundation).  
   - src_assets/ : static web-UI assets (Vue components, HTML/CSS/JS) served by the builtin HTTP server.  
   - third-party/ : embedded external libraries.  
   - CMakeLists.txt & cmake/ : build configuration, cross-platform packaging, dependency detection.  
   - packaging/, docker/, scripts/ : deployment artifacts (AppImage, Flatpak, Dockerfiles), helper scripts.

3. Examine the README for additional insights  
   - Backend features: virtual display creation/removal, permission system, HDR handling, multi-GPU support, input sync, auto-resolution matching.  
   - Web UI for pairing and configuration over HTTP(S).  
   - Integration points with SudoVDA, Artemis (Moonlight Noir), and hardware encoders (AMD VCE, Intel VAAPI, Nvidia NVENC).

4. Drawing the system design diagram  
   a. Main components  
      • Frontend Web UI  
      • HTTP/REST API Layer  
      • Streaming Pipeline  
      • Virtual Display Manager  
      • Encoder/Decoder Module  
      • Input Handler  
      • Configuration & Permission Manager  
      • Logging & Metrics  
      • Platform Abstraction Layer  
      • Third-Party Modules (exploded)  
      • External Clients (Artemis/Moonlight, Web Browser)  
      • Host Hardware (GPU, Audio, Network)  

   b. Relationships & interactions  
      1. Web Browser ←→ HTTP Server: configuration, pairing, status.  
      2. Artemis Client → RTSP/HTTP Pairing → Streaming Pipeline.  
      3. Streaming Pipeline ←→ Virtual Display Manager → Host GPU/Driver.  
      4. Encoder Module (NVENC/VAAPI/VCE/Software) ←→ Platform Abstraction ←→ Hardware.  
      5. Input Handler ←→ Network ←→ Client → Platform Abstraction → inject into virtual display.  
      6. Config & Permission Manager consulted by all modules for access control.  
      7. Logging & Metrics sink events from core modules.  
      8. Third-Party Modules are linked into their respective components (see below).

   c. Architectural patterns & design principles  
      - Modular layers: HTTP/API, streaming, hardware abstraction.  
      - Dependency injection for platform adapters.  
      - Thread-pool & event-driven design for concurrency.  
      - CMake-driven plug-in of third-party libs.  
      - Resource ownership via RAII and move-semantics.

   d. Key technologies & libraries  
      - HTTP Server: Simple-Web-Server  
      - JSON handling: nlohmann_json  
      - Encoding: NVENC SDK (nv-codec-headers), Intel VAAPI, AMD VCE  
      - Graphics: Glad (OpenGL), DirectX HLSL shaders  
      - Virtual Display: SudoVDA, libevdev, Wayland, X11, AVFoundation  
      - Buffering: TPCircularBuffer  
      - Input: inputtino, ViGEmClient  
      - Testing: googletest  
      - Build: CMake, Docker, Flatpak, AppImage  

5. Tailoring the diagram to Apollo’s architecture  
   - Emphasize separation of the Web UI (static assets) from the native C++ server core.  
   - Show platform-specific submodules under a “Platform Abstraction” container.  
   - Detail the streaming pipeline: capture → buffer → encode → network → client.  
   - Illustrate virtual display lifecycle: create via SudoVDA (Windows) or equivalent on other OS, attach encoder, remove on stream end.  
   - Highlight permission system controlling client access to launch apps, input, streams.

6. Exploding Third-Party Modules  
   - Create a dedicated “Third-Party Modules” section in the diagram and draw individual boxes for:  
     • Simple-Web-Server (HTTP layer)  
     • nlohmann_json (config, API payloads)  
     • Boost (where used)  
     • TPCircularBuffer (stream buffering)  
     • ViGEmClient/SudoVDA (virtual display driver)  
     • inputtino (input abstraction)  
     • libevdev (Linux input)  
     • glad (OpenGL function loading)  
     • nv-codec-headers & NVENC SDK (Nvidia encoding)  
     • moonlight-common-c (Moonlight protocol support)  
     • googletest (unit tests, can be shaded off as “Test Harness”)  

   - Draw arrows from each third-party box to the core module that uses it.

7. Diagram styling guidelines  
   - Label each component clearly.  
   - Use directional arrows for data/control flow (e.g., HTTP requests, video frames, input events).  
   - Color-code by layer:  
     • UI (e.g., blue)  
     • API & Control (e.g., green)  
     • Streaming & Encoding (e.g., orange)  
     • Platform & Drivers (e.g., purple)  
     • Third-Party (e.g., gray)  
   - Use distinct shapes:  
     • Rectangles for modules  
     • Cylinders for persistent storage (config, logs)  
     • Clouds for external clients/services  

8. Final checklist for the diagram  
   - All major components identified and labeled.  
   - Platform-specific adapters grouped but detailed.  
   - Third-party modules exploded and linked.  
   - Clear data flows: control (HTTP/API), media (video/audio streams), input.  
   - Technology names annotated.  
   - Permission and config manager centrally located.  
   - Host hardware and external clients represented.  
   - Legend explaining colors/shapes.  

By following these instructions, you will produce a comprehensive, accurate, and Apollo-specific system diagram that captures the essential architecture and incorporates every third-party module in context.  
</explanation>
